title: The Post plantation brothers, one white and one mulatto
summary: Playing a New Year's job with Lucky Roberts in South Carolina, a white man proudly called the mulatto stable manager his brother.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: music. And speaking about that way of life, I went to play with the Post family in South Carolina. They were a very rich people who conditioned race horses, you send your horses down there to be conditioned. It's an old southern family. And there were two fellows who met us at the train -- this was with Lucky Roberts and there were about five -- four or five of us to play his New Year's gig down there. Just for one night. Two fellows -- one was a mulatto sort of Negro and the other was a white man. So, I happened to be in the car with the white man and the rest of the boys -- well, there was two or three in my car and there was two or three in the other car with this mulatto Negro. So, this white fellow says, "See that fellow driving that car over there?" He said, "That's my brother. That's Charlie Post. There ain't a better man that ever walked this green earth. That's my brother over there. His daddy was my daddy." Now, that situation is all over the South in those days. We saw it very prevalent in the south,and in Greenville, Mississippi, and Charleston, South Carolina you saw that. The Posts -- the mulatto Posts had charge of all the servants and horses and stables. He ran that. He had his separate house on the plantation. He didn't live in the big house, but he said, "There ain't a better man ever walked this green earth, and that's my brother." And he was a Negro.
Well, we were saying, that's their way of life (unintelligible)
The way of life -- that's why I brought that up, because -- and they understood it. They understood it.
